steps: The centromeres divide, separating the sister chromatids.
The spindle fibres pull the separated chromatids towards opposite poles of the cell.
Each chromatid is now considered a daughter chromosome.
items.finalAnswer: During anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell.

steps: The centrosome duplicates and the two centrosomes move towards opposite poles of the cell.
They organise the spindle fibres that attach to chromosomes and help move them during cell division.
items.finalAnswer: The centrosome organises the spindle fibres that move chromosomes during cell division.

steps: Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of a chromosome joined together at the centromere.
They separate during anaphase II of meiosis.
items.finalAnswer: Sister chromatids are identical chromosome copies joined at the centromere; they separate during anaphase II.

steps: Regeneration is the process by which an organism replaces or regrows lost or damaged body parts.
Mitosis produces new cells for this process.
The new cells grow and develop into the cells and tissues needed to replace the lost or damaged part.
items.finalAnswer: Mitosis produces the new cells needed for regeneration of lost or damaged body parts.

steps: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
The nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear, and spindle fibres form as the centrosomes move to opposite poles.
Metaphase: Chromosomes arrange themselves at the equator of the cell.
Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres of the chromosomes.
Anaphase: The centromeres divide, and sister chromatids separate.
Spindle fibres pull the daughter chromosomes towards opposite poles of the cell.
Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles and become less distinct as they uncoil.
Nuclear membranes form around each group of chromosomes, and the spindle fibres disappear.
items.finalAnswer: Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, in which chromosomes condense, align, separate and form two nuclei.

steps: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.
In animal cells, the cell membrane pinches inwards to form a cleavage furrow, which deepens and divides the cell.
In plant cells, a cell plate forms in the middle of the cell and grows outwards until it joins the cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.
items.finalAnswer: Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow, while plant cells form a cell plate that grows outwards.

steps: Mitosis is responsible for the growth of an organism by increasing the number of cells.
It replaces worn-out or damaged cells and helps in the repair of tissues.
It enables regeneration of lost or damaged body parts in some organisms.
It is a means of asexual reproduction in many organisms.
It maintains the chromosome number and genetic similarity in the daughter cells.
items.finalAnswer: Mitosis is important for growth, repair, replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction, while maintaining chromosome number.

steps: Prophase I: Chromosomes condense and become visible, and homologous chromosomes pair up to form bivalents.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
The nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear, and spindle fibres form.
Metaphase I: Homologous chromosome pairs arrange themselves at the equator of the cell.
Spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes.
Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles; the centromeres do not divide.
Telophase I: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes may form around them.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, producing two haploid cells.
items.finalAnswer: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair and cross over, align at the equator, separate to opposite poles and form two haploid cells.
